armed_with_private_reach.description:
Issue #56. Could whoever last ARMED this schedule — created it, re-timed
it, resumed it, or scheduled its workflow — reach private work? A run
reads it back ([`scheduled_run_refusal`]).

Who records it:
* The daemon's schedule routes, from their caller
(`routes::session_reach::schedule_reach`) — `Some(true)` or `Some(false)`.
* `/loop`, `/schedule` and `platform__manage_schedule`'s `create`, from the
CHAT that made the schedule, because the schedule acts for that chat and
`create`'s card promises "on this chat's model": `Some(true)` when that
chat runs a private model, `None` otherwise (never `Some(false)`, which
would refuse the schedule once a person moves that chat to a private
model).
* A person's proof-backed approval of `platform__manage_schedule`'s
`unpause` — `Some(true)`, exactly as the desktop's Resume button.

What each value lets a run do:
* `Some(true)` — the person at the keyboard, or a caller or chat on a
private model. Its runs may bind whatever model they resolve.
* `Some(false)` — a caller that could reach only public work. The routes
admit such a caller only to a schedule whose runs resolve a PUBLIC model
at that moment, but a run resolves its model again when it starts. So a
run that would bind a private model on such a record is refused before
it starts, and says so in [`Self::last_error`]. Measured before this
field existed (independent QA, 2026-09-14): with only the daemon secret,
re-time a schedule made from a public chat to every minute, delete that
public chat, and the next tick started a new chat on the private default
with nobody present.
* `None` — nobody who could reach private work is recorded as having armed
it: a public chat's `/loop`, a CLI with no daemon to ask, the daily
meditation, or any row written before this field. It runs on the model
it resolves EXCEPT one: when the chat it was made from no longer gives a
model (deleted, unreadable, or recording none) and the run would fall
back to a PRIVATE default ([`RunModelSource::DefaultInPlaceOfCreator`]).
Deleting a public chat takes nothing but the daemon secret, so without
that exception the QA chain above needed no arming request at all: one
`DELETE /sessions/<public creator>` turned every such schedule's runs
private (independent QA, 2026-09-14, on this branch — ticks created
`scheduled`/`versa_azure`/`private` chats with an empty `last_error`).

⚠ The file is not a boundary, and this does not pretend otherwise: a shell
that can write `schedule.json` can write `true` here, which is the residual
`docs/deployment/programmatic-session-access.md` records.

Written only by the `_armed` mutations below and by the creating surfaces
named above; every other writer leaves it as it found it.

creator_session_id.description:
Issue #56 (§9.3 C2). The chat this schedule was created from, when there
was one — `/loop` and `/schedule` always have one; a workflow scheduled
from the CLI or the schedules route does not.

A scheduled run resolves its provider from THIS session's recorded
`provider_name` before falling back to the global default (see
[`resolve_scheduled_provider`]). Without it a job created from a chat on
a private model silently runs on the user's commercial default — R5 —
and, once the design's §6.3 rule that a `Scheduled` session inherits its
creator's classification lands, Gate A would refuse the bind on every
tick forever.

last_error.description:
The last run's failure, kept ON THE JOB so the schedules UI can show it.

A cron tick that returns `Err` used to leave nothing behind but a log
line, and a scheduled run mints a fresh session each time, so there was
no surface anywhere that a repeating job had been failing since the day
it was created. Cleared by the next successful run.

max_runs.description:
Optional cap on total firings. When `Some(n)`, the job auto-pauses once
`run_count` reaches `n` — the bound that keeps `/loop` from running
forever. `None` = unbounded (durable `/schedule` jobs).

owns_source.description:
Did the scheduler write [`Self::source`] itself, and may it therefore
delete that file when the job goes?

⚠ Written by [`Scheduler::add_scheduled_job`] from its `make_copy`
argument and by nothing else — a value supplied at a construction site is
overwritten, so callers pass `None` and let the scheduler answer.

⚠ `Option`, not `bool`, and the third state is the whole point. A job
persisted before this field existed deserialises as `None`, and the two
creation paths that produced those rows are indistinguishable from the
row alone: `POST /schedule/create` and `biorouter schedule add` copied the
workflow and own the copy, while a schedule added from a workflow row
points straight at the user's own file. `false` for both would strand
every legacy copy; `true` for both would delete a user's workflow. `None`
says "unrecorded", and [`scheduler_owns_source`] answers it from where the
file actually lives.

run_count.description: Number of times this job has fired. Used to enforce `max_runs`.

SecretBody.description:
The Crew vault's passphrase (`POST /crew/credentials/init` and `/unlock`), and nothing
else. The launcher supplies the request's separate user-action key automatically.

oneOf.description: An extension's own environment, keyed by extension name.

SecretDestination.description: Where the trusted surface must put the values it collects.

SecretKeyRequest.description: One credential a [`ActionRequiredData::SecretRequest`] card asks for.

description.description: Optional help text: where to get the value, what format it takes.

key.description: The name it is stored under — an env var name, a keyring entry.

label.description: What the field is called on the card.

required.description: Whether the request can be satisfied without this one.

ServerAccess.description:
What a connection's agents can do on its server, as this computer learned it at the
connection's last verified connect (design OW-6): the workspace server's capabilities and the
person's own bridge's `bridge.hello`. Served as a saved connection's `server_access`, so
Connection settings can say what is missing (an older server, an older bridge, a kernel that
cannot confine commands) before anyone tries. Display only: a full-access run is offered
only when both say so, and the broker and the bridge enforce it.

bridge_version.description: The person's own `biorouter-crew` on the server; `null` when it predates `bridge.hello`.

confined_execution_available.description:
The bridge can confine commands to a work folder (the server's kernel has Landlock ABI
3 or later); `null` when the bridge is older and does not say.

full_access_available.description:
The workspace server takes full-access runs (`remote_access_v1`) and the person's own
bridge can run commands as their account (`remote_full_v1`).

home.description: That account's home folder on the server; `null` when it did not say.

landlock_abi.description: The server kernel's Landlock ABI, as the bridge read it; `null` when it did not say.

user.description: The server account the bridge runs as; `null` when it did not say.

ServerStorage.description:
A workspace server that has stopped saving changes (its disk or quota is full, or it could
not write its storage), as its `hello` says since W2-BRK-3. Reading still works; every
change is refused until the host frees space and restarts Crew (T3-BE-13). Served as a saved
connection's `server_storage`, so a person is told before trying to write, not after.

code.description:
Why: `storage_full` (the server's disk or the account's quota is full) or
`storage_failed` (another storage error).

since.description:
When the server stopped saving, in seconds since the Unix epoch, as it says; `null` when
it did not say.

state.description: Always `storage_failed`: the server has stopped saving changes.

accumulated_total_tokens.description:
Lifetime totals. New usage writes use the four-bucket billed total;
databases created before billed-bucket accounting may contain legacy
context totals here, so reporting and budgets use `token_events` instead.
These counters grow without bound, so SQLite and Rust both use 64-bit.

branch_point_msg_uid.description:
The durable `msg_uid` of the exact parent message this session was
branched at — the divergence point (BR-45). Paired with `diverged_from`
(parent session), it is the edge label of the branch forest. `None` for
normally-created sessions. Anchoring on this stable id instead of a
whole-second timestamp is what fixes the same-second over-truncation.

decision_count.description:
How many decision-model calls this chat has made (its rows in the
`decisions` table), for History's per-chat count. Filled by the full
listing (`GET /sessions`, `biorouter session list`) only, and only when
the chat has at least one; `None` everywhere else, so absent means
"none, or not counted here". Decision calls can number in the thousands,
which is why History shows this one number and never a row per call.

diverged_from.description:
Id of the session this one was diverged (branched) from, if any. Set by
`diverge_session`; `None` for normally-created sessions. Lets the UI show
a session's lineage ("branched from …").

parent_session_id.description:
Id of the parent session that spawned this one as a subagent (BR-71).
Sibling of `diverged_from` (branch lineage): `diverged_from` records a
user fork; this records a delegation. `None` for non-subagent sessions.
It is what the interface groups tabs by, and what
`refuse_unless_direct_subagent_child` reads to keep a delegation-scoped
grant pointed at its own children. It is NOT read by the §7 capability
matrix any more: that matrix had an `L` axis until lineage stopped being
a boundary for writes (issue #56).

privacy_reason.description:
Audit and UX only — never read by a gate. One of `turn:<provider>`,
`mcp:<extension>`, `inherited:<parent_id>`, `diverged:<parent_id>`,
`backfill:<provider>`, `declassified_by_user`. §12.4 grades the
declassification confirmation on whether it has ever been `mcp:*`.

It therefore holds the **dominant** provenance, not the first or the
latest one: the storage layer lets an `mcp:` raise displace a non-`mcp:`
reason and lets nothing displace an `mcp:` reason. Freezing it on the
first raise would answer "has it ever been `mcp:*`" with a flat no, since
Gate B's `turn:*` always lands before Gate C's `mcp:*`.

total_tokens.description:
The *current* turn's usage — the live context-window occupancy. Bounded by
the model's context limit, so `i32` is safe.

SessionClassification.description:
CLASSIFICATION — the most sensitive thing a session has ever touched.

`Ord` is derived and `Public < Private`, so `max` is the accumulation and is
spellable. Monotone in time; the storage layer refuses to lower it (see
`SessionUpdateBuilder`'s `CASE WHEN` emission).

recentTurns.description: Newest turn first, at most [`RECENT_TURNS`] turns.

has_more.description:
Paged form only (`limit` was sent): whether the listing holds more rows
after this page. Absent from a whole-list answer.

next_cursor.description:
Paged form only: where the next page resumes. Pass it back as `cursor`,
unchanged, and do not parse it; it is the same token `GET
/sessions/sidebar` issues. Absent on the last page.

sessions.description: List of available session information objects

SessionMetaChanged.description:
What changed about one chat's row.

⚠ **Advisory, exactly like the frame in `/reply`.** It is not a session
payload and no gate consults it: `privacy_tier` here is a REPORT of a
classification the daemon has already committed, and a consumer that wants
to act on it re-reads the row.

model_name.description: `model_config_json`'s `model_name`, as the row now holds it.

privacy_reason.description: The row's classification provenance, as stored.

provider_name.description: `provider_name` as the row now holds it.

revision.description: The revision this change was stamped with.

truncated.description:

PARTIAL history. Applying it and believing yourself current is the stale

SessionModelUsageResponse.description:
Per-model token breakdown for one session. Each row carries its dollar
cost priced on the server per request (cache rate and long-context tier

"unknown" bucket (turns recorded before model attribution, or providers
that reported no model).

SessionSkillsRequest.description: Add and remove are applied to **this** conversation only.

add.description:
Skill (or bundle) names to enable for this conversation, even where the
machine-wide preference has them off.

remove.description:

machine-wide preference has them on.

The catalog after the write, plus the override that produced it.

Returning the whole catalog rather than an acknowledgement is deliberate: it
is what lets the interface render confirmed state instead of the optimistic

sessionAdd.description:
The persisted `workspace_skills/v1` value, echoed so a caller can tell a
per-chat deviation from a machine-wide default without re-deriving it.

SessionState.description: How one session deviates from the machine-wide answer for a given skill.

SessionSubagents.description: Everything a surface needs to draw a chat's subagents and its phase plan.

diverged_from.description:
BR-45: the session this one was branched from, or `None`.

Carried on the SUMMARY, not just on the full [`Session`], because the
sidebar draws a glyph per chat kind and had no other way to know. Its
only remaining signal was the default branch NAME (`"… (branch 2)"`),
which anyone can rename away: of the branches on this machine, one in
five had been renamed and so drew as an ordinary chat.

parent_session_id.description: BR-71: `sub_agent` rows are grouped under this parent in History.

session_type.description: BR-71: the session's type as stored (`user`/`scheduled`/`sub_agent`).

billingSessionId.description:
The chat whose limit and spend this is: the chat itself, or a
subagent's parent.

chatDollarLimitInert.description:
A per-chat dollar limit is set but nothing the chat used is priced, so
it cannot fire.

monthDollarLimitInert.description:
A monthly dollar limit is set but nothing this month is priced, so it
cannot fire.

paused.description:
A limit is reached: the chat makes no model request until it is raised
or lifted (or, for the month, the next local month begins).

pausedByEstimate.description:
`paused` because the next request is estimated to pass the limit named
by `reason`, not because it is reached.

warn.description: A limit is at 80% or more and none is reached.

clear_primary.description:
Forget the primary *at this scope*: the session then has no primary
even while the machine-wide default names a base. Mutually exclusive
with `primary_kb` and `inherit_primary`.

hidden_kbs.description:
Replace this scope's hidden list — i.e. redefine the session's set.
Omit to leave the set alone. `[]` is an explicit "hide nothing here",
not a request to inherit the machine-wide list.

inherit_primary.description:
Drop this scope's own primary preference. A session then follows the
machine-wide choice; at machine scope this restores Biorouter's shipped
Soul default. This is the way back from `clear_primary`, and the only
way out of the explicit "no primary" that deleting a session's pinned
base leaves behind. Mutually exclusive with `primary_kb` and
`clear_primary`.

kb_id.description:
Deprecated alias for `primary_kb`, kept for one release so a stale
renderer bundle talking to a fresh daemon keeps working. Follows the
same rule: omitted leaves the pointer alone, `null` forgets it — which
is exactly how such a bundle clears.

primary_kb.description:
Make this base the session's primary — the KB-less write target. It
must be a member of the **resulting** set, so `hidden_kbs` in the same
body is applied first. Omit to leave the pointer alone; send `null` to
forget it (the same as `clear_primary`).

maxTokens.description: With `limit`: billed tokens this chat may use, a whole number above 0.

maxUsd.description: With `limit`: priced dollars this chat may use, above 0.

sha256.description: Its SHA-256, as 64 lowercase hex digits.

source.description:
`bundled` (part of this app) or `dev` (a development copy from
`BIOROUTER_CREW_BROKER_DIR`).

target.description: The platform it is built for: `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`.

code.description:
The SSH codes (`crew_ssh_auth_required`, `crew_ssh_key_refused`,
`crew_ssh_host_key_unknown`, `crew_ssh_host_key_changed`, `crew_ssh_unreachable`,
`crew_bridge_missing`, `crew_broker_not_running`, `crew_ssh_failed`), a connect's
(`crew_workspace_identity_mismatch`, `crew_request_refused`), or one of setup's own:
`crew_setup_cancelled`, `crew_setup_timed_out`, `crew_setup_sign_in_expired`,
`crew_setup_server_unreadable` (the server's answer could not be read),
`crew_setup_start_failed` (Crew did not start the workspace; see `outcome.host`, and
`detail` for what Crew printed), `crew_host_storage_unsafe` (other accounts can write to
a folder above where the workspace is kept; `detail` lists them one per line, and
`fix_storage_permissions` lets setup fix the ones the account owns),
`crew_host_name_in_use` (the account already hosts a workspace of that name or in that
folder: open it, or start it when it is stopped), a join's or a save's own codes after a
host's `finish` saved the workspace (`outcome.connection_id` and `outcome.steps_left`
say what is left),
`crew_setup_changed` (the connection's login or route changed while the job ran),
`crew_install_artifact_unavailable`, `crew_install_unsupported_platform`,
`crew_install_dependency_missing`, `crew_install_incompatible` (the program there does
not run or name its version), `crew_install_unexpected_target` (a link, a folder or
another account's file where the program goes), `crew_install_checksum_tool_missing`,
`crew_install_no_space`, `crew_install_permission_denied`, `crew_install_busy` (another
install in the account), `crew_install_transfer_incomplete`,
`crew_install_checksum_mismatch` (nothing was replaced) or
`crew_install_outcome_unknown` (the connection dropped after the transfer; set up again
to check).

detail.description: The server's or OpenSSH's own bounded words, for Copy details.

host.description: The SSH hop a connect failure concerns.

message.description: One plain sentence for a person.

SetupInstalled.description: The account's Crew program, as the check found it.

problem.description: Why it cannot be used or replaced, for a person.

runnable.description: Whether `--version` ran and named a version; `null` when there is no file.

SetupOutcome.description: What a job did, once it is done.

connection_id.description:
A member's connection, connected and verified; or the connection a host's `finish`
saved, set as soon as it is saved, so a job that stops after the save still names it.

context_draft.description: The first context document, drafted from the server's facts (Markdown).

context_revision.description: A host's `finish`: the revision of the context document it saved from the draft.

allOf.description: A new workspace's governance after a host's `finish`.

host_command.description:
The start command that ran, character for character: the Host dialog's, with `--create`
on the start line.

The `Ord` derive is load-bearing: `Low < Medium < High < Unknown`, so an

confirm.description:
Issue #56 Task 30. The typed confirmation Settings → Privacy sends with a
write to `BIOROUTER_PRIVACY_TIERS`, and nothing else sends at all.

⚠ **What this is and what it is not.** It is a **UX guard against an
accidental or model-composed config write**, not an authorization
boundary: the phrase is a fixed string in the shipped source, so a caller
holding the daemon secret replays it. That is acceptable because
`check_token` has no principal — the daemon cannot tell Settings →
Privacy from any other loopback caller — and because the *authorization*
on this route is `X-User-Action`, not the phrase. What the phrase buys is
that the flip cannot be a side effect of an ordinary `/config/upsert`,
which is the reachable path: a model *can* compose one of those through a
tool.

⚠ **This comment used to justify the phrase by adding *"and a caller that
already holds the secret can raise its own session to private capability
anyway"*, citing AR-15. That is no longer true and is withdrawn** —
AR-15 was retired on 2026-08-02 by DR-16 (commit `0757823f`), which made
an upward provider bind require `X-User-Action`. Do not restore the
argument: the guard does not need it, and a stale "we are already open
here anyway" is how a weakened control gets waved through.

UsageReportRow.description:
One bucket of the usage report.

`date` is present unless grouping by [`UsageGroup::Model`]; `modelId` is
present unless grouping by [`UsageGroup::Day`]. `cost` is the dollar cost of
the priced turns in the bucket, or `None` when *every* contributing turn was
unpriced (an unknown model) — a `null` cost never means "$0". `hasUnpriced`
flags a bucket that mixes priced, unpriced, or incomplete turns, so a day
cost can be read as "at least this much" rather than exact.

Decision-model requests count in the tokens and the priced cost, never in
`turns`; they are counted in `decisionRequests` and broken out in
`decisions`. An unpriced request to a local Ollama decision model counts as
$0 and does not set `hasUnpriced`: an automatic local decision model would
otherwise mark almost every month as "at least". An unpriced Baseten
decision request was billed, so it does set it.

cacheReadTokens.description:
Prompt-cache read/creation tokens in the bucket. `None` preserves
historical incompleteness; it must not be presented as a measured zero.

costExcludesCache.description:
`true` when cache cost is omitted because a contributing model has no
cache rate or an event did not report a required cache bucket.

decisionRequests.description: Decision-model requests in the bucket, which `turns` leaves out.

allOf.description:
The decision-model share of a usage bucket: the requests whose provider is a
decision provider (`providers::decision::chat::is_decision_chat_provider`),
shown as their own line.

Its tokens and priced dollars are already inside the bucket's own totals,
so the totals still match the provider's meter. Its requests are not: a
decision request is not a model turn, and the bucket's `turns` leaves it
out.

cost.description:
Dollar cost of the priced decision requests, or `None` when none is
priced. Never "$0" for unknown: `hasUnmetered` and `hasUnpriced` say
which kind of unpriced request is behind a `None`.

hasUnmetered.description:
`true` when at least one request went to a decision model with no
meter (a local Ollama model). It cost nothing, so it is "not metered",
never "unavailable".

hasUnpriced.description:
`true` when at least one request went to a hosted decision model
(Baseten) Biorouter has no price for, or reported incomplete counts:
the provider billed it at a rate Biorouter does not know. Unlike the
bucket's own `hasUnpriced`, it says nothing about the chat totals.

totalTokens.description: Billed tokens, or `None` when a request behind it reported neither count.
Billed tokens, or `None` when the bucket includes incomplete history.

api_key.description: The daemon's secret key. Biorouter's server is loopback-only and authenticates every route with this header except two: /status, and /tool_bridge/{nonce}, which is not part of this API at all. The bridge is an MCP endpoint a coding-agent child process calls, its path carries a single-turn capability nonce instead of a header (Codex sends no Authorization header), and it is deliberately absent from this spec because no Biorouter client should ever call it.
